3	## KeyPoints
4	
5	Question Is service in the US military associated with suicide risk among those with disability?
6	
7	Findings In this survey study with selfreported cross-sectional data from 231 099 US adults, representing more than 236 million individuals, service in the military was associated with higher suicide risk among those without disability. However, among those with disability, military service was associated with lower suicide risk compared with nonveterans with disability.
8	
9	Meaning These findings suggest that military service could be a protective factor against suicide among a subpopulation of US adults.

19	## Introduction
20	
21	Suicide is a leading public health concern. In 2020, there were nearly 46 000 suicide deaths with more than 1.2 million suicide attempts. 1 Suicide was listed as the 12th leading cause of death, at a rate of 13.48 per 100 000 people, with men at greatest risk. 1 Also in 2020, 4.9% of US adults reported suicide ideation, 1.3% suicide planning, and 0.5% attempting suicide. 2 Suicide and self-directed injury have high costs to society that extend beyond the emotional toll of losing individuals to a preventable cause of death. Notably, suicide behaviors cost more than $1.3 trillion/y in lifetime medical and work-loss expenditures. 3
22	
23	Amongthose at heightened risk for suicide are people with disability. Indeed, a recent US population-based study demonstrated that the presence of any disability impacting function was associated with a greater likelihood of reporting suicide ideation, suicide planning, and attempting suicide, with risk increasing as the number of disabling limitations increased. 4 Unfortunately, and as observed in the literature, 5 subgroups of people with disability at most heightened risk for death by suicide are not well known. Within the disability population, veterans of US military service are overrepresented, 6 likely due to exposure to injury and death during service. The most common physical disabilities among veterans include tinnitus, hearing loss, and motor deficits. 7 Veterans are also overrepresented in the population of individuals who die by suicide. In 2020, 6146 veterans died by suicide with an unadjusted rate of 31.7 per 100 000 people. 8 This is over twice the general US population suicide rate, 1 with elevated risk among veterans consistently observed over a 19-year period. 1 As of 2020, suicide was the 2nd leading cause of death among service members and veterans younger than 45 years, and the 13th leading cause among all veterans. 8 In sum, veterans are at greater risk for having a disability and for experiencing heightened risk for suicide relative to nonveterans. However, little is known about how veteran status may moderate the effect of disability status on risk for suicide-related outcomes.
24

input.text: In 2020, there were nearly 46 000 suicide deaths with more than 1.2 million suicide attempts. Suicide was listed as the 12th leading cause of death, at a rate of 13.48 per 100 000 people. Also in 2020, 4.9% of US adults reported suicide ideation, 1.3% suicide planning, and 0.5% attempting suicide. In 2020, 6146 veterans died by suicide with an unadjusted rate of 31.7 per 100 000 people. Test-specific significance levels were assessed at alpha <= .05. Multicollinearity was assessed using the variance inflation factor but was not detected. The final sample included 231 099 participants, representing 236 551 727 US adults (weighted), of whom 20.03% (weighted n = 47 397 876) reported a disabling limitation. Of those with limitations, 60.5% reported 1 limitation, 21.7% reported 2 limitations, and 17.8% reported 3 or more limitations. Risk for suicide was reported by 4.39% (weighted n = 10 401 065), with 69.71% reporting suicide ideation only, 18.19% reporting suicide planning, and 12.10% reporting suicide attempt. Veterans represented 8.92% of the sample (n = 13 859; weighted n = 21 111 727; 16.0% aged 35-49 years; 91.0% men; 6.7% Hispanic; 10.9% non-Hispanic Black; and 78.4% non-Hispanic White), and 91.08% were nonveterans (n = 217 240; weighted n = 215 440 000; 25.4% aged 35-49 years; 44.0% male; 16.5% Hispanic; 11.7% non-Hispanic Black; and 63.3% non-Hispanic White). Among those reporting no disabling limitations, veterans were 71% more likely to report planning relative to nonveterans (AOR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.17-2.49). However, among people reporting 1 disabling limitation, VWD had 43% lower odds of planning compared with nonveterans (AOR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.34-0.95). Also, among people reporting 2 disabling limitations, VWD had 54% lower odds of attempt compared with nonveterans (AOR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.24-0.88).

findings.location: Table 3, Nonveteran / >=3 Limitations, suicide attempt (vs suicidal ideation only), AME column

problems: the estimate 0.04 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-0.01, 0.05] (expected about 0.0200)
the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0090, but p = 0.07 is reported

findings.notes: The single clearest internal inconsistency in the paper, and it fails on two independent grounds. (1) The AME point estimate 0.04 is not the midpoint of its own interval [-0.01, 0.05]; the midpoint is 0.02. Even allowing full 2-dp rounding on all three printed values, the attainable midpoint range [0.015, 0.025] does not reach the estimate's rounding range [0.035, 0.045]. (2) The p recovered from that interval is 0.009, which contradicts the p = .07 printed on the same row. Every one of the other 20 AME rows in Table 3 IS centred within rounding (verified by inspection against this same criterion), so this is an isolated cell, not a systematic convention. The accompanying AOR on the same row, 1.36 (0.98 to 1.89) with p = .07, is fully self-consistent (checked separately, `ame_row_aor_control`), which localises the error to the AME interval rather than to the underlying model: a single mis-set digit in the upper bound (e.g. 0.09 printed as 0.05) would reconcile the row. Reported as suspicious, not impossible -- 0.04 does lie inside [-0.01, 0.05], so no arithmetic law is broken, and a transcription/typesetting error is the most parsimonious reading. Warrants a correction request.

computed.direction: mixed -- 4 recovered p above the printed value, 5 below

findings.notes: Nine of the 50 odds ratios have a p recovered from their own CI that differs from the printed p, in every case by less than 0.016 -- i.e. by less than one unit in the second decimal place at which these p-values are printed. Three points argue strongly for benign rounding rather than an integrity problem, and the editorial stage should weight them accordingly. (a) The direction is MIXED (4 up, 5 down); a paper shifting p-values toward significance would show a one-directional pattern. (b) The recovery uses a normal approximation, whereas the paper used SAS PROC SURVEY on a stratified multistage CLUSTER sample, where Wald intervals use a t-multiplier on design degrees of freedom rather than 1.96 -- this alone displaces recovered p at exactly this magnitude. (c) The CI bounds are themselves printed to only 2 decimals, so the recovered SE carries visible quantisation. Two of the nine (AOR 1.61, p=.04 and AOR 0.49, p=.04) do carry paper claims, and both sit adjacent to the .05 threshold, so they are worth naming individually; but neither crosses it under either reading. Recorded at the tool's severity for completeness, with the caveat that this cluster is most likely reporting precision, not anomaly.

findings.location: Results, 'Suicide Ideation, Planning, and Attempt by Veteran and Disability Status', final sentence
findings.quote: No significant differences in risks for suicide were observed by veteran status among people reporting 3 or more disabling limitations.

reported.claim: no significant differences by veteran status at >=3 limitations

findings.notes: The paper states a null for the most severely disabled subgroup, and this is not a throwaway -- it is the boundary condition on the abstract's protective claim. All three intervals are wide enough to be compatible with substantial effects in BOTH directions: up to a 1.58-fold difference for ideation, 2.03-fold for planning, and 3.13-fold for attempt. The attempt interval [0.32, 1.45] is especially uninformative; it is equally compatible with veterans at >=3 limitations having a third the odds of attempt and with them having half again the odds. 'Not significant' here reflects a small veteran cell (the paper itself concedes 'smaller cell sizes after stratifying sample groups'), not demonstrated equivalence. Returned indeterminate rather than as a flag because the paper states no smallest effect size of interest, so equivalence cannot be tested -- that refusal IS the result. The wording 'no significant differences ... were observed' is defensible as written; it would become a misstatement if read as evidence that military service confers no benefit at high disability burden.

findings.location: Method, 'Statistical Analysis'; Tables 1, 2 and 3
findings.quote: Test-specific significance levels were assessed at a <= .05.

inputs.additional_untested_families: eTables 1-4 in Supplement 1 (not available to this sweep)

findings.notes: The paper explicitly adopts a per-test alpha of .05 with no multiplicity adjustment, across at least 68 enumerated tests in the main tables alone (50 AORs plus 18 Table 1 bivariate comparisons), before counting the four supplementary eTables. This is not itself an error -- uncorrected reporting is common in descriptive epidemiology -- but it bears directly on which conclusions survive, because the paper's protective-effect narrative rests on results clustered just under the threshold: p = .03 (AOR 0.57), .02 (AOR 0.46), .04 (AOR 1.61), .04 (AOR 0.49), .01 and .02 (Table 3 nonveteran rows). The veteran-vs-nonveteran contrasts that carry the abstract form a family of 12 in Table 2 and 8 in Table 3; a Bonferroni-type adjustment within either family would retain only the strongest (AOR 0.31, p = .002) and drop the rest. The count is reported here; the editorial stage should decide how much weight to place on it. Note this is an enumeration of the paper's own reported tests, not a recomputed statistic.

findings.location: Key Points (Findings and Meaning); Abstract; Conclusions
findings.quote: service in the military was associated with higher suicide risk among those without disability. However, among those with disability, military service was associated with lower suicide risk compared with nonveterans with disability.

reported.claim_scope: unqualified, across 'those with disability' and all suicide outcomes

findings.notes: The Key Points and abstract state two directional conclusions without qualification, but the underlying comparisons are mostly null. For the protective claim among people WITH disability, 2 of the 9 veteran-vs-nonveteran contrasts in Table 2 are significant (planning at 1 limitation, attempt at 2 limitations); the other 7 are null, and NONE of the three contrasts at >=3 limitations -- the most disabled group -- reaches significance. The two significant results also fall at different disability levels for different outcomes, with no consistent gradient. For the elevated-risk claim among people WITHOUT disability, 1 of 3 contrasts is significant (planning, AOR 1.71), while ideation (1.12) and attempt (0.98) are flat. The direction of every significant estimate does match the claim, so this is over-generalisation of scope rather than misstatement of direction; the numbers are correctly reported in the tables. Flagged because the Key Points is the part of a JAMA Network Open paper most widely read and least qualified.

findings.quote: Among those reporting no disabling limitations, veterans were 71% more likely to report planning relative to nonveterans (AOR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.17-2.49) (Table 2), but this was not significant in sensitivity analyses (eTable 3 in Supplement 1).

inputs.abstract_claim: service in the military was associated with higher suicide risk among those without disability

findings.notes: The Key Points assert that military service was associated with higher suicide risk among people WITHOUT disability. Within Table 2 that claim rests on a single contrast, AOR 1.71 for planning -- and the authors themselves report, in the same sentence that introduces it, that it did NOT retain significance in their multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis. The corresponding Table 3 subgroup result (AOR 1.61, p = .04) did retain significance, so the claim is not unsupported; but a headline conclusion whose primary supporting estimate fails the paper's own robustness check, with that failure disclosed only in the body text and absent from the Key Points, is a reporting asymmetry worth surfacing. Credit where due: the authors did report the non-replication rather than suppress it. Note also the reverse pattern -- 'nonveterans reporting 3 or more disabilities were 102% more likely to report attempt in sensitivity analyses only' -- i.e. a result significant ONLY under imputation is also reported as a finding. Claims are being drawn from whichever of the two analyses happens to reach .05.

findings.location: Method, 'Statistical Analysis'; Supplement 1, eTable 3 header (N = 241 675)
findings.quote: Sensitivity analyses were performed with multiple imputation by chained equations for all missing values to assess bias. ... eTable 3. Multiple Imputation Sensitivity Analysis ... (N = 241 675)
findings.notes: The sensitivity analysis is run on N = 241 675, the full adult sample, versus N = 231 099 in the main analysis -- so 10 576 records are restored by imputation. Per the flow diagram this necessarily includes imputing the OUTCOME (suicide ideation/planning/attempt) for 1 141 respondents and the EXPOSURE (disability status) for 2 044, alongside 7 261 with missing covariates. Imputing the dependent variable is generally discouraged (it adds no information about the outcome-predictor association while propagating the imputation model's assumptions into the estimate), and imputing the exposure compounds it. This matters more than usual here because several claims turn on the discrepancy between the two analyses in both directions -- one headline result loses significance under imputation, another gains it. Marked indeterminate rather than suspicious: the imputation model is not described in the available text and eTables 3-4 were not accessible to this sweep, so the magnitude of the concern cannot be established. Flagged for human review of Supplement 1.

findings.notes: The tool returned 'suspicious' (7.8 orders of magnitude below the printed threshold) and I am recording that verbatim, but I do NOT carry the flag forward, for reasons that are decisive here. STALT detects concealment -- a small study hiding an implausibly extreme p behind 'p<.05'. Neither condition holds. The analytic sample is 231 099 respondents weighted to 236 million; recovered z-values across the p<.001 rows run from 6.7 to 13.4, which is the ordinary consequence of that sample size acting on genuinely large disability-suicide associations, not of an implausible effect. Nothing is concealed: the AOR and its 95% CI are printed alongside, and the magnitude is recoverable from them by exactly the arithmetic used here. Capping at '<.001' is JAMA house style. Escalating this would be a textbook false positive on a large-N epidemiological paper.

findings.notes: Recording a deliberate non-application, because running these tools here is the most likely route to a false accusation on this paper. GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT all require observations that are integers over an integer denominator. Every percentage in Table 1 is survey-weighted: its denominator is a sum of sampling weights, not a count of people, so a weighted percentage is not of the form k/n and GRIM-family granularity arguments simply do not hold -- applying them would manufacture impossibilities from entirely ordinary cells. The paper reports no means and no standard deviations at all, so GRIMMER and SPRITE have no input. reconstruct_2x2 was also declined: the unweighted cell counts needed to rebuild a 2x2 are never printed, and the weighted percentages cannot substitute. This is a genuine coverage gap driven by the paper's design, not an oversight.

inputs.design: cross_sectional observational; veteran status is self-reported exposure, not an allocated arm

findings.notes: Declined deliberately. Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher and the Bayesian dispersion test detect groups MORE similar than randomisation permits; both presuppose that allocation was random, so that baseline p-values should be Uniform(0,1). Here nothing was randomised -- veteran status is a self-reported characteristic, and the two groups are expected to differ profoundly (91.0% vs 44.0% male, 48.8% vs 17.8% aged 65 or over). The observed pattern of uniformly LOW p-values is the substantive finding that motivated covariate adjustment, and the rulebook's red flag (uniformly HIGH p-values, tau-hat > 1) is not even definable in this design. Running either test would be a category error producing a meaningless verdict. The absence of a baseline-similarity finding in this report reflects the design, not a clean result on a test that was performed.
findings.reproduction_problem: Recorded as a non-application. The command is shown to document what was declined; csf_test refuses non-randomised designs by construction, so it yields a refusal rather than a verdict, which is the intended outcome here.

findings.notes: The tool returned 'suspicious' (7.8 orders of magnitude below the printed threshold) and that is recorded verbatim, but I do NOT carry the flag forward, for reasons that are decisive here. STALT detects concealment -- a small study hiding an implausibly extreme p behind a threshold. Neither condition holds. The analytic sample is 231 099 respondents weighted to 236 million; recovered z across the p<.001 rows runs from 6.7 to 13.4, the ordinary consequence of that sample size acting on genuinely large disability-suicide associations. Nothing is concealed: the AOR and its 95% CI are printed alongside and the magnitude is recoverable from them by exactly the arithmetic used here. Capping at '<.001' is JAMA house style. Escalating this would be a textbook false positive on a large-N epidemiological paper.

findings.notes: Recording a deliberate non-application, because running these tools here is the likeliest route to a false accusation on this paper. GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT all require observations that are integers over an integer denominator. Every percentage in Table 1 is survey-weighted: its denominator is a sum of sampling weights, not a count of people, so a weighted percentage is not of the form k/n and GRIM-family granularity arguments do not hold -- applying them would manufacture impossibilities from entirely ordinary cells. The paper reports no means and no standard deviations at all, so GRIMMER and SPRITE have no input. reconstruct_2x2 was also declined: the unweighted cell counts needed to rebuild a 2x2 are never printed, and weighted percentages cannot substitute. A genuine coverage gap driven by the paper's design, not an oversight.

findings.location: Table 1, 18 P values comparing veterans with nonveterans
findings.quote: Table 1. Sociodemographic and Clinical Characteristics of 231 099 Respondents, Representing 236 551 727 US Adults, by Veteran Status

inputs.design: cross_sectional observational; veteran status is a self-reported exposure, not an allocated arm

findings.notes: Declined deliberately. Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher and the Bayesian dispersion test detect groups MORE similar than randomisation permits; both presuppose random allocation, so that baseline p-values should be Uniform(0,1). Nothing was randomised here -- veteran status is a self-reported characteristic and the groups are expected to differ profoundly (91.0% vs 44.0% male, 48.8% vs 17.8% aged 65 or over). The observed pattern of uniformly LOW p-values is the substantive finding that motivated covariate adjustment, and the rulebook's red flag (uniformly HIGH p-values, tau-hat > 1) is not even definable in this design. Running either test would be a category error yielding a meaningless verdict. The absence of a baseline-similarity finding in this report reflects the design, not a clean result on a test that was performed.
findings.reproduction_problem: Recorded as a non-application. The command documents what was declined; csf_test refuses non-randomised designs by construction, so it returns a refusal rather than a verdict -- which is the intended outcome here.

findings.notes: No a-priori power or sample-size calculation is stated, so verify_power_analysis cannot run -- only alpha is given; effect size and target power are both absent. This is unremarkable for a secondary analysis of an existing national survey, where N is fixed by the data source. It is recorded because it bears on interpretation elsewhere: the paper's own limitations concede 'smaller cell sizes after stratifying sample groups to veteran and nonveterans', and the widest intervals in Table 2 (e.g. attempt at >=3 limitations, 0.32 to 1.45) fall precisely where veteran cell counts are thinnest. Precision within strata, not overall sample size, is the binding constraint on the null results.

No field benchmark in the tool's cited set applies to adjusted ORs from national survey epidemiology, so the check was declined rather than forced.
